transcript.text: I am the operations lead at a tour company. Each month I tell our local partners how many guides to reserve in each destination for the month after next. If I reserve too few, we hire freelancers at the last minute for about three times the price; if I reserve too many, we pay a small fee for each guide we do not use. My director asked me for a machine learning model that forecasts how many bookings we will receive per destination each month. The table I shared is our booking export up to late February 2026: one row per booking with the booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, whether it had free cancellation, and whether it was cancelled. I will use the result myself every month to fix the reservation. [shares bookings.csv]

Your ask is clear, so here is how I read it before you pick. The real problem isn't forecasting bookings, it's forecasting the bookings you can still see on the day you commit. A model trained on finished months and asked to predict a month two months out would look excellent and then miss the part of the curve it was never allowed to see. The second thing your table shows is that demand and guides aren't the same number: 22.9% of bookings cancel, and it ranges from 18.9% in Paris to 26.2% in Dubai, so per destination the cushion differs. What I'd do: build the target as a snapshot — count only bookings with booking_date at or before the cutoff for each travel month and destination — and validate it by replaying past months, never a random split. Plan: (1) clean and confirm the 12 rows under a destination called TEST are test data; (2) build the point-in-time monthly series per destination, dropping travel months after March 2026 as incomplete; (3) fit a forecast and backtest it month by month against actuals, checking it beats the naive rules; (4) translate the forecast plus its error into a guide count using your freelancer price against the idle fee. Two options are below: the forecast itself, or the same model scored on your cost asymmetry so it tells you how many guides, not how many bookings. Which one fits what your director expects to see?

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)

choices.title: Cost-aware guide reservation model
choices.what: You get: A recommended number of guides to reserve per destination each month, deliberately biased to the side that costs you less, with the money saved versus your current rule estimated from the backtest. Trade-off: Needs one number from you (the fee per unused guide, as a share of the guide price) and the output is a recommendation, harder to explain to your director than a plain forecast. Effort: Slightly more than option 1; same build.

choices.title: Baseline first: how wrong is your current call?
choices.what: You get: A chart plus a number for the error of the naive rule. That is the bar a model has to beat, and it tells you whether a model is worth building at all. Trade-off: No forecast is produced; you would still need one of the options above to act monthly. Effort: Fastest - questions against the table, no build.

transcript.text: I am the head of marketing at a subscription company. The board asked for an AI segmentation of our customers, and I would like five or six segments with names we can put on a slide. The table I shared has one row per customer: signup date, the segment we already record, city, plan, tenure in months, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and whether they churned the next month. Next quarter my team can run at most three email campaigns: one to move people to a higher plan, one to keep people who look likely to leave, and one welcome series for new customers. The same person should not receive two of them. My campaign managers will use the segments to decide who gets which campaign. [shares customers.csv]

I read your table before choosing anything, and three things shape the options. Your recorded segment won't carry a slide: it only splits customers into business (239) and consumer (961), and their churn rates are 14.6% and 18.1% — nearly the same people. Plan says far more: basic customers churn at 22.4% (603 of them, averaging 19.22 a month), plus at 11.1%, premium at 14.5%. That spread is where both the save campaign and the upgrade campaign live. Support tickets in the last 90 days sit almost flat across plans (1.12 to 1.21), so tickets alone won't separate anyone, and I checked: no column looks written after the churn outcome, so nothing is leaking the answer. One thing to flag, as an assumption you can correct: welcome is a small job here. Only 53 customers have tenure of three months or less, out of 1,200. So the segments will mostly decide upgrade versus save, and welcome will be a thin slice defined by signup date rather than behaviour. I'm also reading churned_next_month = 1 as "left the following month", and I'd keep that column out of the clustering itself so the groups describe behaviour and we use churn only to check and name them. The three options differ in kind: clusters found by the algorithm and then mapped to your campaigns, a churn-risk model whose score becomes one of the segment axes, or plain thresholds on the fields you already record. The second answers "who looks likely to leave" most directly; the first gives the board the cleanest picture. Which one fits the slide you have to defend?

choices.title: AI segments, then map each to one campaign
choices.what: Cluster the 1,200 customers on tenure, monthly spend, support tickets, plan and city (churn kept out of the clustering and used only to check the result), pick between five and six groups, and name each one from what defines it. Then assign every segment to exactly one campaign so no customer can appear twice. You get: Five or six named segments with a one-line profile each, size, average spend, ticket load and measured churn rate, plus a ready-made segment-to-campaign table for the slide and for your managers. Trade-off: Clusters describe behaviour, not intent: a segment can be large and obvious yet hold few savable customers, so the campaign mapping needs your judgement on the middle groups. Effort: One run today, then a short pass with you on the names.

choices.title: Churn-risk score first, segments on risk x value
choices.what: Train a model on churned_next_month to score every customer's likelihood of leaving next month, then cut the base into five or six segments from two axes: predicted risk and spend. High risk plus high spend goes to the save campaign, low risk with room above their plan to upgrade, newest signups to welcome. You get: Segments whose borders are a number each manager can filter on, a measured accuracy from a holdout you have not seen, and a straight answer to who looks likely to leave. Trade-off: Two steps instead of one, and it takes longer to explain on a slide; the board sees a model, not a cluster picture. Effort: A model build plus a segmentation pass, checked against a holdout.

choices.title: Rules from the fields you already record
choices.what: Six fixed buckets built from plan, tenure and spend thresholds (for example long-tenure basic, young plus, high-spend premium), with counts, spend and churn per bucket from the table as it stands. You get: Numbers you can defend word for word in ten minutes, and a rule your managers can apply without any model to trust. Trade-off: It is not AI and it finds nothing the columns do not already say: your existing segment split only says business or consumer, and those two differ by barely three points of churn. Effort: Quick, in this chat.

Your plan column does most of the work: basic churns at 22.4% across 603 people, plus 11.1%, premium 14.5%, so "at risk" and "ready to move up" both live inside basic. Tickets look flat (1.12–1.21 across plans), so I'll only use them if the high-ticket tail actually churns worse — I'll check before committing. Rules run in priority order, so nobody lands in two campaigns. One question: when you say new customers for the welcome series, do you mean the last three months of signups? Only 53 of 1,200 sit in that window, so if your welcome series really covers six months I should widen it before I set the cuts.

Now I'll size each rule bucket exactly as the campaign manager will apply it — in priority order, so the counts can't overlap.

Here is the ladder I'm using. It runs top to bottom, and the first line a customer matches is the only one they land in — so nobody can be claimed by two campaigns, which was your hard constraint. 1. **New on Ramp** — tenure 0–3 months → Welcome series. 2. **Friction Flagged** — 3 or more support tickets in the last 90 days → Save. 3. **Ready to Step Up** — high tickets cleared, spending at the top of their current plan band (basic at 25 and above, plus at 55 and above) → Upgrade. transcript.text: I am a data scientist at a company that sells accounting software to small firms. Two years ago we built a model that scores every new lead on how likely it is to become a customer, and the sales team calls the highest scores first. Since the autumn the sales team says the top leads are much worse than they used to be, and my manager wants me to retrain with a larger model and more features. Some context on the data: since the summer, part of our leads comes from a partner marketplace; we moved to a new CRM in August, and two form fields the model uses are no longer collected; and finance now counts a lead as converted when a free trial starts, where before it was the first payment. I have the old training set and every lead since, not yet exported. What would you do?

I'll record what you've told me before I answer.

You've described three changes that happened at once, and only one of them is a model-fitness problem. Retraining bigger, with more features, fixes none of the other two and usually makes the third worse. The target moved. The old model was trained to rank leads by probability of first payment. Finance now calls a lead converted at trial start. A small-firm lead that starts a trial and never pays is now a "win," and one that pays after a long trial is no longer what gets counted. Any measured decline in lead quality may be a redefinition, not a decay. The population moved too: marketplace leads arrive with different intent, firm size and price sensitivity, so they can flood the top decile and degrade what sales actually sees on the phone while overall AUC still looks fine. And the inputs moved: since August, whatever the pipeline fills into those two missing fields is what the model scores on. So diagnose before you retrain:

1. Prove the degradation on the slice sales touches — precision@top-N per month, calibration, and score distributions — cut by lead source and by pre/post-August, on a time-based holdout rather than a random split. This needs the export with stored score, timestamp, source, and outcome dates. 2. Rebuild both labels on the overlap. If the model still ranks first-payment well but trial-start looks bad, the problem is the definition, not the model. 3. Audit the surviving features for drift and check what the new CRM puts in the two discontinued fields. 4. Only then retrain — on one consistent label, evaluated on the most recent months — and decide whether marketplace leads need their own threshold or their own model. 5. Stop rule: if step 1 shows no drop on the original label, don't spend the quarter on capacity. One thing changes my plan most: going forward, which event should the score rank — trial start, first payment, or both as two scores?
Everything I know is in what I wrote. Choose what you judge best and go ahead.

I've started the answer as advice rather than a project, because the honest next move isn't training anything — it's proving which of your three changes caused what sales is reporting. Once the diagnosis has numbers, the retrain becomes a project. Here is what I decided and what you should do. A trial-start label rewards the model for finding people who click "start free trial," which is exactly the kind of lead a marketplace feeds you. Rebuild that one label from raw event dates for every lead, in both CRM eras, rather than trusting each era's stored "converted" flag. 1. Export one row per lead: lead date, source/channel, the score the model actually gave it plus model version, the current contents of the two discontinued fields (including blanks), trial-start date, first-payment date, revenue. 2. Measure the claim, not the feeling: precision@top-N per month, split by source and by pre/post-August, on the original payment label. A time-based holdout, never a random split. 3. Compare labels on the overlap. If the model still ranks payments well and only the trial-start view looks bad, the definition changed, not the world. 4. Audit feature drift on the survivors, and find out what the new CRM writes into the two missing fields — a default fill there can quietly dominate the score. 5. Retrain only if steps 2-4 show real decay, on the single payment label, evaluated on the last three months, and decide then whether marketplace leads need their own threshold. Stop rule: if step 2 shows no drop on the payment label, don't spend the quarter on capacity — give your manager the measurement instead.

transcript.text: I am the credit risk manager at a consumer lender that finances phone and appliance purchases in shops. Today a rulebook written by our underwriters approves about 40 percent of applications. Management wants to grow, so they asked me for a machine learning model that predicts default for every applicant, to replace the rulebook and approve more people safely. We have about 60,000 past loans with the application form, the bureau score and whether the loan defaulted within 12 months, and I can export them next week. For the applications we rejected we kept the form and the bureau score, nothing more. The model would decide each new application automatically at the shop counter. How should I go about it?

[DCLab drew a dashboard above this message]

Here's the honest read: management hasn't asked for a model, they've asked you to approve more people without breaking your loss rate. The model is only one half of that; the other half is where you cut it off. And the trap in your data is this — your 60,000 loans are the 40% the rulebook let through. Train naively and the model will be most confident and most wrong exactly in the band you're expanding into. So the deliverable is a score plus a decision rule plus evidence about the reject zone — not a model that "replaces the rulebook" on day one. The plan I'd follow:

1. **Build the base right.** One row per application, only fields known at the counter (your bureau-null and no-bureau-thin cases are informative — keep them as their own category, never fill with averages). Only mature vintages, and validate out-of-time on the newest months, not randomly. 2. **Beat the bureau score, not nothing.** Two models: bureau score + amount + tenor as baseline, then the boosted-tree version with the full form. If the full model adds no lift in AUC/KS *and* calibration over the score alone, the rulebook isn't what's holding you back, and that's a valuable finding. 3. Management picks a point on that curve. That is the decision they actually own. 4. **Get honest risk on rejects.** A small random over-approval of rulebook-rejected files at modest limits gives real labels and stands up to a regulator far better than reject inference, which rests on assumptions you can't test. If that's impossible, do inference with a sensitivity band. 5. **Ship as challenger.** Shadow decisions for two to three months, then raise the cutoff in steps, monitoring first-three-payment default (your fast signal — 12 months is too slow to steer on) and score drift. Two flags: the economics in this design (default base rate, cost per default, margin per loan) are placeholders until you give me your real figures, and nothing is computed yet since the export isn't here. When management says "approve more safely," is there a number behind it — a target approval rate, or a ceiling on losses you must not cross?

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)
Everything I know is in what I wrote. Choose what you judge best and go ahead.

[DCLab drew a dashboard above this message]

The deliverable this week is the export, not the model. Give it one row per application — approved and rejected — with the date the form was received at the shop, not the booking date, and the default column left blank for rejected files. Keep the bureau score's missing states distinct: thin-file and not-obtained mean different things, so never fill them with an average. When the file arrives, my order is bureau-only baseline first, then the full model, tested on the newest applications and judged by calibration as much as by ranking. Then a curve of approval rate against loss rate, for management to pick their line on — shipped as a challenger, never a silent takeover.
